newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Fiji risks Beijing ire with Taiwan pact.
newsitem.headline: Fiji risks Beijing ire with Taiwan pact.

text.p: The Pacific island nation Fiji, a diplomatic ally of China, signed a mutual-recognition communique with Taiwan on Friday, risking friction with the Nationalist-ruled island's communist rival.
"The status is just below establishment of diplomatic relations," Foreign Minister John Chang told reporters after the signing ceremoney.
"(The pact) recognises us as an official government and a sovereign nation. We feel this is very important," Chang said.
Taiwan's exiled Republic of China government has diplomatic ties with only 30 states, mainly in Africa and central America. The rest of the world recognises Beijing's communist government.
Beijing has regarded Taiwan as a renegade province since a civil war split them in 1949 and refuses to recognise any country that has official ties with the island.
There was no immediate reaction from Beijing.
"What matters is not how Taiwan describes relationship but what China says," said a western government representative in Taipei. "I would be surprised if Beijing didn't respond."
Chinese parliament chief Qiao Shi was quoted on September 9 in the party flagship People's Daily as hailing Fiji's "one China" stance and wanting more cooperation with Pacific states.
The Taiwan-Fiji communique was signed by Chang and Fijian Foreign Minister Filipe Bole, who arrived in Taipei on Thursday for a five-day visit.
Chang said his ministry would push for full diplomatic relations with the former British possession in the South Pacific.
Foreign ministry officials said Fiji was the third state to enter into this kind of "mutual recognition" pact with the Republic of China government.
Pacific neighbours Vanuatu and Papua New Guinea, both of which also recognise China, signed similar agreements with Taiwan in September 1992 and May 1996, respectively.
A foreign ministry statement said Bole would discuss setting up a trade office in Taipei during his stay.
Taiwan has provided agricultural assistance to Fiji since 1978 and opened a trade office there in 1987.
Beijing in August won the latest round in its battle with Taipei for diplomatic allies, wooing back Niger four years after the African state switched ties to Taiwan.
